summary: Specifies a way to bind a visual image of a certificate to an X.509 public key certificate by defining an otherLogos image type under RFC 3709. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 9399.

eli5.summary: Lets a digital ID card carry a picture, such as a logo, so people can recognize who it belongs to.

subtitle: Attaching visual representations to X.509 certificates.

tldr.problem: X.509 certificates store identity information as text, but people cannot easily interpret them—they need to know which issuer is trustworthy, who the certificate belongs to, and what it is for. Text attributes alone do not convey this clearly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6170 adds a way to bind a visual image (logo, seal, or full certificate representation) to a certificate by extending RFC 3709's logotype extension with a new otherLogos type that can hold PDF, SVG, or PNG images.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now display certificate images to help users recognize and trust certificates. This was later superseded by RFC 9399, which consolidated certificate extensions.

today: RFC 6170 defined certificate images as an extension to RFC 3709 logotypes in 2011. The specification was later superseded by RFC 9399, which consolidated X.509 certificate extensions and logotype processing. Certificate images remain part of modern X.509 implementations, though adoption has been limited; most deployments continue to rely on text-based certificate attributes and separate branding mechanisms.

sections.title: The Challenge of Certificate Identity
sections.content:
X.509 certificates (as defined in RFC 5280) store identity information for cryptographic keys. They contain fields like organizationName, commonName, country, and serialNumber. But these text fields present a semantic problem: an application reading a certificate does not know which fields are important, how to label them to the user, or even what they mean.

For example, when a person needs to check a certificate—to confirm a website's identity, validate a software signature, or select which of their own certificates to use—they must understand and evaluate text attributes. This is difficult without out-of-band knowledge. RFC 3709 introduced the logotype extension to bind images like company logos to certificates. RFC 6170 extends this by defining a new type of logotype: a full certificate image that provides a complete visual representation chosen by the certificate issuer.

The certificate image can show all information the issuer thinks is relevant for a typical user: the certificate context (its purpose), the issuer's identity, and the certificate subject's identity.
sections.eli5: Text on a certificate is hard for people to understand. A certificate can now carry a picture that the issuer designed to help you understand: who it came from, who it belongs to, and what it is for.

sections.title: Certificate Images and Logotypes
sections.content:
RFC 3709 defines a general logotype extension that can hold company logos, community symbols, or other images. Each type is identified by an Object Identifier (OID). RFC 6170 adds a new image type: certificate image, identified by OID id-logo-certimage.

When a certificate image is included, it MUST be a complete visual representation covering three aspects:

  • Certificate Context: visual marks or text that help a user understand the intended purpose and typical use of the certificate.
  • Certificate Issuer: identity of the issuing Certificate Authority.
  • Certificate Subject: identity of the certificate's owner or purpose.

The issuer decides what information—text, symbols, colors, graphics—makes up a complete visual representation. However, the visual meaning of Issuer and Subject information MUST match the textual representation in the certificate itself. Applications with a graphical user interface MAY use the certificate image as the sole visual representation of the certificate.
sections.eli5: A certificate image is like a designed poster that shows the certificate's story: 'This is from a trusted company, it belongs to this person, and it can be used for this purpose.'

sections.title: Image Storage and Metadata
sections.content:
Images can be referenced by URL or embedded directly in the certificate using the data URL scheme (defined in RFC 2397). The LogotypeDetails structure holds the media type (MIME type), a hash of the image data, and one or more URIs.

When a certificate image is included with optional metadata (LogotypeImageInfo), the xSize and ySize fields specify the recommended display size in pixels. If these differ from the actual image size, the image SHOULD be scaled while maintaining the aspect ratio. The language field (using RFC 5646 language tags) indicates any text or audio language within the image.

The hash value binds the image data to the certificate's signature: if anyone modifies the image, the hash no longer matches. This ensures the image comes from the issuer and has not been tampered with.
sections.eli5: The certificate keeps a fingerprint of the image so that later on, people can verify the image wasn't changed. You can also store a suggested size and language information.

sections.title: Supported Image Formats
sections.content:
RFC 3709 requires support for JPEG and GIF. RFC 6170 adds three more formats:

  • PDF: A Portable Document Format document, following the PDF/A profile (application/pdf MIME type). PDF is useful for formal, document-like certificate representations.
  • SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics, using the SVG Tiny 1.2 profile. SVG provides resolution-independent graphics and can include text. SVG images MUST NOT reference external resources (IRI references of type B, C, or D) or contain scripts. When embedded in a certificate using the data URL scheme, SVG MUST be GZIP-compressed as SVGZ format.
  • PNG: Portable Network Graphics, the recommended bitmapped format (image/png MIME type).

Implementations MUST support JPEG and GIF, and SHOULD support SVG. Compliance with these formats ensures compatibility across applications.
sections.eli5: The picture can be a PDF document, a scalable drawing (SVG), or a regular image (PNG, JPEG, or GIF). Different formats work for different needs.

sections.title: Security and Trust Concerns
sections.content:
RFC 6170 inherits all security considerations from RFC 3709. The principal concern is that a malicious or careless Certificate Authority could include false, conflicting, or misleading information in a certificate image. For example, a CA might embed a logo in graphical form that contradicts the text attributes, or include malicious data that exploits bugs in image rendering libraries.

SVG images present particular risks: if an SVG image references external data, the hash only covers the URI reference, not the referenced content. Clients SHOULD verify that SVG images meet the security requirements (no external references, no scripts) and reject non-compliant images.

Applications must use up-to-date image rendering libraries to safely process potentially malicious image data. CAs must be careful when accepting graphics from certificate requestors, especially if the certificate signing algorithm is vulnerable to collision attacks. Relying parties must carefully select which CAs they trust.

Certificates and their images are typically public, but privacy-sensitive information may occasionally be included. Organizations using certificate images with such information should implement appropriate access controls.
sections.eli5: A bad CA could hide misleading information in the picture. Or a picture could have a virus or trick that breaks image viewer software. Everyone involved—the CA, the image software, and the person trusting the certificate—needs to be careful.

items.title: PDF
items.text: Document-style, follows PDF/A profile for long-term preservation.

items.title: SVG
items.text: Vector graphics, scalable, must use Tiny 1.2 profile without external refs.

items.title: PNG
items.text: Bitmap image, recommended format, good compression.

items.title: JPEG/GIF
items.text: Required formats from RFC 3709, widely supported.
